one_liner: Demo BLAKE3 file hasher in C/C++ that reads through io_uring and beats Rust b3sum on cold-cache NVMe reads.
what_it_does: Two small command-line programs (liburing_b3sum_singlethread.c and liburing_b3sum_multithread.cc) that compute the BLAKE3 hash of one file or block device and print it. They take eight positional arguments: block size in KiB, queue depth, O_DIRECT on/off, ring-buffer cell count, and IOSQE_IO_DRAIN/IOSQE_IO_LINK toggles. This is not a library. The article presents it as a template: replace the blake3_hasher_update call with your own block-processing function to get an in-order streaming reader.
how_it_is_fast: A fixed ring buffer of aligned blocks, each cell in one of three states (requested, available, consumed), lets io_uring keep 2-4 sequential reads in flight while the consumer hashes completed blocks in file order with the single-threaded C BLAKE3 (AVX2/SSE dispatch). Using O_DIRECT with large blocks (512 KiB) skips the page cache copy, so on the author's machine, where hashing (about 4.26 GB/s cached) is faster than the disk (about 3.55 GB/s), the run is bound by disk speed. The multithreaded version puts the io_uring submit/complete loop and the hasher on separate threads, synchronised with atomics, and stays fast without O_DIRECT.
when_to_use: Hashing large files once each from fast NVMe on Linux, where you want disk-limited throughput and do not want to fill the page cache (single-threaded build with O_DIRECT).
As a reference or starting point for an in-order io_uring streaming reader (checksums, parsers, uploaders) that must consume blocks sequentially.
On machines where single-core BLAKE3 is faster than the disk; there it matches cat/fio line rate (10 GiB in 2.899 s, about 3533 MiB/s).
Learning io_uring queue-depth and block-size tuning: the article includes BS/QD sweep tables and an instrumented build that counts requests in flight.
when_not_to_use: When the file is already in the page cache, or the CPU hashes slower than the disk reads: the C BLAKE3 has no multithreading, so Rust b3sum with multiple threads (or mmap) may win.
When you need a maintained tool or library: 7 commits, last activity 2023-08, no tests, no packaging, hashes only one file per run (batch mode is an open enhancement issue).
Non-Linux platforms or kernels without io_uring; the hand-written libblake3.a recipe in the README is x86-64 assembly only.
Network or FUSE file systems where short reads can happen: the program prints 'panic: short read' and exits instead of reissuing the request.
If you need a LICENSE file: the repo has none, only an SPDX MIT header in the source, which came from the liburing io_uring-cp.c example it modifies.

integration.dependencies: liburing (liburing-dev on Debian 12), BLAKE3 C library built into libblake3.a by hand
integration.min_toolchain: gcc with -D_GNU_SOURCE for the C version; g++ with C++11 (std::thread, std::atomic) for the multithreaded version; Linux kernel with io_uring (tested on 6.1.0-9)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 as documented (the README build uses SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512 .S files); other architectures not documented
integration.thread_safety: Single-use program built on global state; the multithreaded variant uses one producer thread and one consumer thread synchronised with atomics; not reentrant
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — prints the same BLAKE3 hash as b3sum for one file, but takes eight positional arguments instead of b3sum's CLI and has no --check, no multiple-file mode and no stdin input

gotchas: Block size must be a multiple of 4 KiB (assert on ALIGNMENT); the best block size and queue depth depend on the machine (512 KiB/QD 2 with O_DIRECT here, 128 KiB/QD 20 without).
The single-threaded build without O_DIRECT is about 25% slower (0.378 s vs 0.301 s per GiB); use the multithreaded build if you want page-cache reads.
Any read error or short read aborts the program with exit(1); no retry, although the article explains how to add one.
Turning on the IOSQE_IO_DRAIN, IOSQE_IO_LINK or inner-loop options makes it slower, according to the author's tables.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over liburing's own examples or couring when you want a small worked example of an io_uring pipeline that reads in file order with a fixed ring buffer and has published cold-cache numbers. Use liburing itself (or SPDK for kernel-bypass) for production I/O code.
verified_claims_summary: On Debian 12 (kernel 6.1.0-9, ext4, unencrypted NVMe advertised at 3500 MB/s, unnamed AMD64 CPU with AVX2 and no AVX-512), with drop_caches before each run and the median of 10 runs, the single-threaded O_DIRECT build hashed a 1 GiB random file in 0.301 s. Rust b3sum 1.4.1 took 0.386 s with --no-mmap and 0.4105 s with --num-threads 1 (about 1.28x and 1.36x, derived from page data); cat to /dev/null took 0.302 s and fio io_uring 0.3025 s, so the gain over cat is noise and the result is disk-bound.
status_note: Abandoned since August 2023 (7 commits, 3 stars); the source carries an SPDX MIT header but the repo has no LICENSE file, so it is listed as reference-only, and it is small enough to read and re-create.
